newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian pepper prices volatile on supply squeeze.
newsitem.headline: Indian pepper prices volatile on supply squeeze.

text.p: A squeeze in world supplies and sharply increased trade has prompted large rises in Indian pepper prices, officials and traders said on Tuesday.
"The market is very volatile and the volume of trading has gone up enormously," said P. Sethuram, secretary of the Indian Pepper and Spices Trade Association (IPSTA).
Sethuram told Reuters by telephone from IPSTA headquarters in the southern city of Cochin that the number of daily contracts at the pepper exchange had risen to 350 from the normal 140-150.
"(This) is because of a tremendous squeeze in world supplies," Sethuram said. "The Indonesian and Malaysian crop has been lower. Until the end of May India was the only source of supplies."
He said on several days pepper prices had swung widely, forcing the authorities to halt trading.
"Price fluctuations within a day should be in a band of 250 rupees ($7) -- up or down. Once it is pierced we stop trading," Sethuram said.
He said IPSTA would approach the Forward Markets Commsssion to increase the band to 300 rupees from 250 rupees.

India produces about a third of the world pepper crop of 180,000 tonnes. Other major producers include Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam. It produced 62,000 tonnes in 1995/96 (November-October) against 55,000 in 1994/95 and has set a production target of 55,000 tonnes for the current year. Exports totalled about 35,000 tonnes in 1996/97 (April-March) compared with 24,150 the previous year.
Exporter Manikant P Shah of Nitin Spices said "There is an upward tendency in the market."
He said Malabar garbled pepper was quoted for July at 14,300 rupees per quintal (100 kg), August at 15,000 rupees and October at 16,300 rupees.
Sethuram said pepper was quoted in the spot market on Monday at 13,450 rupees per quintal compared with 12,750 rupees a week ago.
Shah said in the five months between January and May, India exported about 33,000 tonnes of pepper and estimated that another 7,000-10,000 tonnes would be available for export in the current season.

He said prices would remain firm with Vietnam having sold most of its crop and the Indonesian and Brazilian crops expected to be lower, and saw Indian pepper prices touching 18,000 rupees by September.
Sethuram said world pepper production is not likely go up significantly in the next few years since it was a tropical crop which could only be grown in a few countries.

The Indian government on Monday said it would hold trial runs in June ahead of the start of the country's first international futures exchange for pepper. Procedural snags had delayed India's ambitious plans to start the exchange by the end of April.
The government did not set a new date for the start of the exchange but Shah expected it to be operational withing the next two months. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
